utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, the 10th of December 2007. My greetings to the OTP representatives, to the Defence counsel and to the accused. We are going to have a witness who is going to testify over two days. I remind you that the witness is called further to the 92 ter proceedings so you will have three hours for your direct examination, based on a report already drafted by the witness and based on his testimony in the Kordic case. I believe there are some 50 documents to be submitted to him. Most of them have already been admitted through other witnesses. After this, the Defence will have three hours and a half, empirically the Trial Chamber thought that Mr. Prlic could have one hour and the other Defence teams would each have 30 minutes, provided of course -- or unless you want to cede some of your time to other teams. So this being said, we should have another witness on Wednesday. But none for Thursday; is that right, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honour, Judge Trechsel, all those in the court and those helping us. Your Honour, yes, I believe that's the case. Given what I know of the schedule now and of the two witnesses this week, I would expect that we would -- could finish on Wednesday. The Court will allow me, I hope, I can't guarantee that. Sometimes we get bogged down in various respects in the courtroom and it might take us longer, but my current expectation is that we will finish the witnesses on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So are we going to finish on Wednesday or Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Perhaps I misspoke. I hope that we will finish on Wednesday. I expect to finish this witness, today's witness tomorrow, I believe the second witness, we should finish the witness on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be briefly heard, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Judge Trechsel, I must convey my disappointment in the Trial Chamber's decision to just give us 30 extra minutes in light of we are dealing with an expert and in light of the fact that his prior testimony is coming in plus new documents plus, plus, plus. I do think that given the nature of the testimony, more time is needed. Now, if Thursday is going to be available, I don't see why, if it becomes necessary, for the next witness to remain a little bit over on Wednesday, why we couldn't handle him. I am just -- I'm not being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the witness, who is to testify to legal issues, constitutional issues and others is of course a witness that will take some time for direct and cross-examination, but given the nature of his testimony, when I said that each Defence team would have 30 minutes, as a rule, in such a situation, like, say, the Defence collectively will appoint one lawyer who may put the questions to the witness collectively and there would be questions of general nature. There is no opposition among the teams as to the merits of this testimony. There shouldn't be any conflict among the Defence teams, so I think it would have been more clever for you to appoint the one lawyer who is going to lead the cross-examination inasmuch as the OTP will have three hours and you will have three and a half hours, amply enough to look into all the problems because 90 per cent of these problems have already been examined through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, thank you for that suggestion and we have taken that suggestion to heart already. My mere observation is as follows: The nature of the testimony is such, and the documents are such, that I don't believe even under the best of circumstances, three and a half hours is sufficient. And I just wish to remind the Trial Chamber that initially the prosecutor indicated that they would merely bring the gentleman over and the report would be admitted and then we would have all the time, two days, for cross-examination. I'm merely suggesting that it may not be enough, even under the most optimal of circumstances but, you know, you've made the decision. I understand it but I simply do not see why we need to cave in to certain witness's whims and fancies, when we do have that extra day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, nobody is caving into anybody's whims. I don't think I'm mistaken. I think that initially the Prosecutor had applied for admission under 92 bis of the expert's, quote unquote, statement and of his testimony in the Kordic case, and the Trial Chamber did not want to harm your rights as a Defence. That's why they called this witness. So stop complaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're giving them everything they asked, plus three hours. That's what I'm trying to convey. That's what I'm trying to convey. They initially said, we want this to come in and the Defence could have cross-examination. You not only say -- and then once you said yes, then they said, well, we want additional documents to come in, plus three hours. That's my complaint. My complain is we went from, more or less, having six hours to now having 3 and a half hours. That's the situation. And I'm not complaining; I'm merely making this observation and I don't think that it is fair. Now I will try my best to do what I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, as to the additional documents, I believe there are five, four of which have already been admitted. I believe there are five documents, four of which have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. His entire testimony is coming in, Mr. President, but I don't wish to argue and waste time but I just wanted to make my observation. I don't think it is fair to the Defence and the Trial Chamber is not doing the Defence any favours by saying the Prosecution can have everything and then limit the rights of the accused. That's what I'm saying. You have given them his prior testimony, you've given them his entire report, you have given them additional documents and you have given them three hours and all you've given us is an additional 30 minutes. To me, it doesn't convey a sense of fairness but perhaps in the end we will be able to manage but I'm merely making that observation and I hope in the future that you will take into consideration our concerns. And this is a major concern. Maybe I'm up to the task. Maybe not. But three and a half hours is certainly a limited amount of time given the breadth and scope of this gentleman's testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Yes, Mr. Scott, do you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please. If it may assist and maybe it will and maybe it won't, I think the Chamber knows by now and I think the Prosecution has been consistent on this, that when a witness who is previously been proposed as a 92 bis witness is -- does come to give viva voce testimony and is essentially then converted into a 92 ter witness, the Prosecution's view in those circumstances is that a limited amount of additional direct examination to highlight some issues is appropriate and I think that's what we've done with a number of these witnesses. As the President rightly points out, most of the exhibits have been used before and we don't anticipate using anything like 50 exhibits with this witness. They were all included because, again, better to have them all than to not have the right ones at the right time, so that there was no confusion and no misunderstanding, all the previous documents related to the witness's evidence were included. But I think at the end of the day the number of documents we will use will be much, much smaller than those on the list and I'm hopeful that we can do it, the Prosecution, I'm hopeful, we will do it in less than the three hours. So of course whatever time we can save that will give the Defence some additional time. Beyond those comments, Your Honour, if the Chamber would allow me there are a couple of other housekeeping matters that I would like to address before the witness comes in, if we could go into private session just for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, you are going to have the floor. I believe you have to give us six IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the OTP has submitted its response to exhibits tendered by 2D, 3D and 6D for witness Amor Masovic. This list shall be given Exhibit numbers IC 736, 737, and 738 respectively. 6D has submitted its response to OTP response to its exhibits tendered through witness Amor Masovic. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 739. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness BB. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 740; the list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 741; the list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 742; and the list submitted by 6D shall be given Exhibit number IC 743. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before the witness comes in I'd like to turn to Mr. Ibrisimovic. Mr. Pusic is not here, as I see. I suppose he's not well. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Let me first check that you can hear me as I'm being translated into your own language. Can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can hear the Croatian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stand up, because you are to read out the solemn declaration but before you do so, could you for the record state your first name, name of -- second name --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ciril Ribicic. I was born on the 30th of June, 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a degree in law. I am a judge of the Constitutional Court of the Republic of Slovenia and professor of constitutional law at the School of Law in Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is going to be my last question. Have you had an opportunity to testify before this Tribunal and if so, in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was seven years ago, I testified in the Kordic case, Dario Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since you are a judge, I don't need to give you much explanation. As you know, we are in an adversarial type of proceeding so you're going to be put questions by the OTP representative, by Mr. Scott, today. I'm sure you've met him already. You met him during the weekend or this morning and following this initial stage, which should take some time, the rest of the day probably, you're going to be cross-examined by the Defence teams. The Judges who are in front of you, there is only two now but usually the Bench is made up of four judges, one of our colleagues has had a sudden death in his family and the other judge is involved in drafting a judgement to be issued on the 12th of December. This is the reason why you have only two judges in front of you but they are going to put questions to you. As a rule, we prefer to put our questions after the parties have asked theirs but sometimes, when you're faced with a document, we like to put questions at that time rather than call up the document later on. So this is, very briefly, what we are going to do. We break every hour and a half. If at any time you do not feel well, you want to have a break, do not hesitate to say so. And if you have a question for the Trial Chamber, equally do not hesitate if you deem it necessary. I'm now giving the floor to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me indicate to the Chamber as well, as we begin, that as I indicated actually a few moments ago, all the Prosecution exhibits that were used with Mr. Ribicic -- or Dr. Ribicic in his Kordic testimony were included among our exhibits should so the record could be complete. We don't expect to use them all. Secondly, in some instances, the same or essentially identical document had already been given a P number in this case. It may have had a different ERN number because as the Chamber probably knows right now for better or worse, there are sometimes more than one copy of the same document. Therefore, in some instances we've used the P number exhibit in this case in lieu of the number in the previous case, the document in the previous case, even though the documents we submit are the same. I thought it was best if we just clarify that at the beginning. Doctor, what is your nationality, please?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I have Slovenian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I just in that last moment or two referred to you as "Doctor" and we discussed this yesterday but I would like to ask you again: You are a constitutional judge, you are a doctor, you are a professor of constitutional law. Is there any particular way that you would prefer that I address you?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Professor will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I should indicate to you, Professor, that the Judges and counsel in the case have been provided with a copy of your curriculum vitae, and while it is certainly quite -- in my submission, quite an impressive curriculum vitae, we will not go through it for purposes of court and the time that we have available to us today, I would like to touch on a few aspects of your background and experience, please. Could you just briefly tell the -- describe to the Judges your formal education?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated from the school of law in Ljubljana. That's where I obtained my Ph.D. On several occasions, I was appointed a professor of constitutional law there. Recently I've been teaching two courses. One at the undergraduate studies and the other at post-graduate studies. Both have to do with the law of the Council of Europe and the European law on human rights and freedoms. I have also been active in politics for quite a long time. At that time, I still had my commitments with the school of law. I was the president of the political party called the League of Communists of Slovenia. During my tour of duty which lasted for three years, that party changed its platform and its name. It left Belgrade and then it appeared at multi-party elections in Slovenia and became a member of the socialist union of modern European socialist parties. Later on for ten years I was a member of the Slovenian parliament and seven years ago, I was appointed a judge of the constitutional court. A few weeks ago I was also appointed vice-president of that court. I have two more years of my -- in my office, and then I will go back to the school of law, and of course I am looking to be retired soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. So just in terms of your judicial position, just to confirm, you have been then a member, a judge of the Constitutional Court of Slovenia since 2000 and the vice-president of that court as of a few weeks ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago some of your political, past political involvements. To what political party did you belong in 1990?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: In 1990, I was a member of the League of Communists of Slovenia, and formerly of Yugoslavia. And I also became the president of that party pursuant to the programme that was drafted by a working group under my leadership and that programme was known under the name Europe Now. We presented that programme at the 14th congress of the Communist Party in Belgrade. Our idea may have been naive at that time. I know that we bore badges with the inscriptions, with Yugoslavia into Europe. However, at that congress, we were outvoted on all important issues so it soon became very clear that with the League of Communists, where Milosevic had main say, together with his group, there was no way that Yugoslavia would go in that direction, so we were all clear when we returned from Belgrade that we, if we wanted to opt for that, we had to try and do it on our own, if we wanted to join European integrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Professor, was it at that time in connection with that congress or at some related time that, in fact, the Slovene delegation left the party congress, if you, I guess, one might say walked out from the party congress?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that this is not relevant material. What Slovenia did or did not do is not relevant. If we are going to go into that I would need additional time because I believe this gentleman was involved in drafting the Slovenian constitution which made Slovenian's constitution above the constitution of Yugoslavia, in other words, the federal constitution was subordinated to the Slovenian constitution. And so if we're going to get into that then I'm going to need to go into this gentleman's background because one of Slovenia's activities during that period was also undermining the federal constitution which this gentleman was responsible for, which led to the break-up of Yugoslavia. Frankly, I don't think it's relevant to what is at issue here today. He is here as a constitutional expert to talk about his findings based on his research, not on Slovenia's efforts to break away from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the question you put and which has been objected aimed at knowing in which context Slovenia became independent. Was it? Or was it just by way of an anecdote?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I believe, in response to counsel's comments, it is relevant for the Chamber to hear that Dr. Ribicic was involved, became very closely involved in the formation of the Slovenian constitutional legal system as a result of the developments in the former Yugoslavia which among other things in addition to his formal educational experience gives him particular - in the Prosecution's submission - expertise on the issues of constitutions that were being formed and established in connection with the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia, and in that respect, there is no one more qualified, perhaps, to address those issues than Dr. Ribicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to briefly respond, again, Mr. President, if we go back to 1989, Slovenia drafted a constitution which this gentleman was responsible for when they were trying to break away, where it made the federal constitution of Yugoslavia subordinate to one of its republics, Slovenia. And therefore, that is a whole issue. Now, nobody is questioning the gentleman's qualifications. He's a professor, he's a politician, by and large, his father was a member, an established member of the Communist Party going back to Tito, with sort of a colourful past. So clearly we are not going into those issues. Nobody is challenging -- the gentleman teaches constitutional law. The issue here is his findings with respect to his analysis on documents concerning Herceg-Bosna, not what Slovenia did or what he did. Otherwise, do I want to go into what -- how he drafted the Slovenian constitution subordinating the federal constitution to a republican constitution, because that's unconstitutional and it calls into question the gentleman's integrity. But we are not going into that. We are not talking about the break-up of Yugoslavia. We are talking about Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the Trial Chamber is interested in Herceg-Bosna. Whether Slovenia became independent or not that's a known fact to all. We are interested in Herceg-Bosna. Please direct your question on that. Only I just have one question for the witness. You told us that you were a leading member of the League of Communists in Slovenia. I did not quite understand the League of Communists in Slovenia, was it an autonomous organisation, independent from the Yugoslav one or was it part and parcel of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, where there was Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The League of Communists of Slovenia was an integral part of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia up to the moment when we left the 14th Congress of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, when we walked out of that congress, actually. From that moment on, there was a break-up in the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It certainly was not my intention to spend a great deal of time on those questions but was, the Prosecution thought, relevant background to this witness's testimony. If I can just ask you this final question, sir, did you in fact participate in the creation of Slovenia's constitutional and legal system in connection with the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia? That's simply one question.

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I participated in the procedure, in the analysis that I prepared for the Prosecutor's Office, of this Tribunal, at several places I compare the situation involving Slovenia and the situations that involved Bosnia and Herzegovina and particularly Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir, and that is indeed why we believe that that information is relevant for the Chamber to have but that wasn't exactly my question; my question was narrower than that. Simply, did you in fact participate in connection with the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia in the creation of the constitutional and legal system of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I participated in that and I believe that the most significant document that preceded the drafting of the constitution was an agreement of all the political parties and groups of deputies in the Slovenian parliament on the plebiscite on the independence of Slovenia. This agreement, I signed myself on behalf of my party. Later on, we embarked on drafting the constitution and I cooperated in its drafting as a member of the parliament of the Republic of Slovenia. This was already at the time following the plebiscite, the constitution was adopted, only half a year after Slovenia declared its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Let us move forward in connection with the report that you had prepared in connection with the Kordic case, which the President of this Tribunal, of this Chamber, has asked you about already, and if you have -- you have a set of binders that have been placed next to you there, to your right. And if I could ask you to just look at Exhibit P 08973 or what you'll probably see on the tab is simply 8973. Yes, that's it, but it's upside down. Can you just simply look at that, sir, long enough to -- can you confirm to the Chamber that that in fact is your report that was prepared in connection with your testimony in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the analysis that I actually prepared seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the subjects of that report, as indicated in the first page or two of your report, did those include, for example, whether Herceg-Bosna satisfied the character or had the characteristics of statehood, what the objectives were in the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or whether the Croatian community and later the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, whether that entity or those structures were democratic or mono-national and the significance of the republic and any significant differences, if any, between the community and the republic? Are those some of the topics that you addressed in your report?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I analysed the constitutional issues relative to the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, its organisation and its operations, and I tried to organise some six or seven questions that were given to me before I embarked on my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since I think it's clear that this report was now written sometime ago, have you had a chance in recent days to review that report from beginning to end?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that the gentleman has notes with him. I would like to know what are those notes and I would like to have a copy of them if he's going to be referring to the notes. He's got handwritten notes with him. If he needs them to refresh his memory then obviously he needs to ask permission from the Trial Chamber. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what kind of notes do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are notes, handwritten notes. I wrote them last night after my meeting with the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and I continued to write them until this very morning in my hotel, Hotel Europa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do they deal with -- do they refer to the points in the Kordic report or are these personal thoughts of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. This relates to the questions that may be asked today with regard to my analysis or report, and I have nothing against anyone having a look at those notes, to ascertain the contents, so I actually tried to anticipate some of the topics that might be discussed and I thought that it might be a good idea to write that down, that that would make me feel more secure as I answer my question -- the questions today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would on firsthand suggest that no notes be used, that he use his memory. If he needs any prompting he can look at his report. The report is in already so that's evidence in a sense, so he can look at his report but we would want him to use his independent memory. Secondly, I would like to have those notes but I suspect they are probably in Slovenian and Slovenian is different from Croatian so we are going to be at a disadvantage, we won't be able to read them so that poses a problem but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the language, can your notes be understood by somebody who speaks B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are actually written in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You told us you had nothing against giving the notes to the parties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is your decision, I will not be using them, but the reason why I glanced at them was because I wanted to say what are those things and the way in which I view my analysis seven years later. Of course, this is not something that is contained in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one question raised by my colleague. When you speak to us in your language, what do you speak? Do you speak Slovenian or B/C/S or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my native language is Slovenian but I do understand Croatian, Bosnian, Serbian. I also understand English. But it is easier for me to express myself in Croatian than it would be in English because I'm more familiar with the terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly now currently you are speaking Croatian not Slovenian; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slovenian is quite different and you don't have the interpreters who work with Slovenian here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Although our interpreters are very good at anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But leave your notes aside, put them aside, and do use your memory in order to avoid any problem. So the document is put aside. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The question that I had put to you a few moments ago, Professor, was whether you've had a chance to review your report again in recent days, have you?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Chamber whether that report continues to be your opinion today? That is, is there any statements or opinions in that report that you would wish to change if you were writing that report today or do you continue to stand by that report?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I for the most part stand by that report. As regards my main views, I would present the same views as I did seven years ago, but I would like to make some minor alterations, three of them. I hope that I will be able to remember all three that I wrote down on that little piece of paper. First of all, in my report, I say that for Croats and Croatia, it would have been easier if they had -- if Milosevic, Karadzic and Mladic were to be indicted before this Tribunal. It was written at the time when Milosevic was not yet before this Tribunal. As we all know, things did change in this regard later on. This is one of the things that I wanted to mention. The second concerns the very conclusion of my report, where I say that in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about 200.000 people were killed, and I saw some very serious analyses at a later date. I attended a seminar on Bosnia and Herzegovina's joining the European Union, it was organised and held in Michigan and I saw some very serious analysis presented there indicating that the number of casualties was in fact significantly lower, somewhere around 100.000. And thirdly, in my report, I mention, as a positive example, regarding the treatment of ethnic minorities and the non-Slovenians in Slovenia, so I used Slovenia as a positive example and now I should be more critical of Slovenia because after I already completed my report, the constitutional court ruled on the issue of the so-called deleted people, people who had failed to ask for and get Slovenian citizenship and they were consequently deleted from all the population lists, lists of people with permanent residence in Slovenia and this decision of the constitutional court has not yet been implemented. It will affect 18.000 people but at any rate if I were to write my report today I would be definitely changing that statement that I made in my report. I take this opportunity to do so now then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we take it, then, that with those additions or explanations that otherwise the report which is marked as, in this case, as P 08973, would continue to be the same report that you would prepare today?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Professor, the Chamber as you already know by now of course, the Chamber and the Defence have your report as well as your prior testimony, and of course we will not go through every word of your report in court. I will ask you some questions about certain parts of the report and of course the Defence may have questions and likewise the Judges may have questions about things in your report that they would like to ask you about. So that's the basic way we will proceed. Before I do ask you a few questions about your report, let me also ask you about your Kordic testimony and if you look in the binders, I believe if you look at what will be marked as Exhibit P 10355 [sic], and again you're likely to find the tab that is 1355. I see you have it there and I think I can represent to you that that is a transcript of your Kordic testimony, both the direct examination and the cross-examination. Have you had a chance to review your testimony prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've read this over the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to the best of your memory and ability, can you say that that again that transcript is an accurate reflection of the testimony you gave in the Kordic case, to the best of your knowledge and memory?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was a very good translation of what I actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a very brief question. In your testimony in the Kordic case, we have the transcript here and we've known it for a long time because the documents were part of the 65 ter list, page 14305, no need for you to look at it, at a given point in time you were asked a question regard -- about Mr. Prlic. Judge May told you this: He asked you whether you had an opportunity to speak to Mr. Prlic, and you then answered that you were willing to answer only in private session. Judge May then said, [In English] There is no need. [Interpretation] In other words, he did not grant you that request. Why did you mention this? Did you know Mr. Prlic or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was preparing this report, I talked with several people who I thought were in a position to give me some information, and to share their views with me on this issue. I mentioned that in my report, and this was discussed before the Tribunal. And I promised them that I would not be using what they had told me in court but that I would only use it as their personal assistance for my preparations. I sent them some questions in writing, and then we had a discussion based on those questions. I asked for this issue to be discussed in closed session so that I could honour the promise that I had given to these people. And I have to say that as I sit here, I no longer have the notes that I had taken during those interviews because I had moved house in the meantime, and I simply don't have this written material and I cannot refer to it. The only thing at issue at that time was whether Dr. Prlic was one of the people who had assisted me in this manner in preparing this analysis or report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did he help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say, to be quite honest, that I don't know after seven years whether he did or not but I do believe that I had a brief meeting with Mr. Prlic and that he helped me -- that Professor Zdravko Tomac helped me organise that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before I -- just to touch again on some of the background matters of your report and given the language issue, before I ask you some questions about your report, sir, consistent with what we have been talking about so far this afternoon in reference to language, did you prepare your report originally in the Croatian -- using the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote the report in Croatian. Of course, it was then translated by the translation -- translators at this Court and I agree with what you've just said, that they are very good translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On their behalf thank you as well. Let me then ask you to go to page 6 of your report. When I'm referring to your report, I may not say it on every occasion but it is Exhibit P 08973. And in the Croatian version, I believe you'll find it at page 5. I've tried as much as I can, I hope, to find the page references for both the English and the Croatian. And in page 6 of the English version and I believe page 5 of the Croatian report, you make this statement, you say: "For an analysis of the emergence of new states in general and of the character of the HZ HB, the most important attributes of statehood are territory, population (sovereign and effective) governance and direct subordination to international law (as a measure of independence), that is being an international -- sorry, my mistake. Let me look because I made a note. I apologise. My note has found its way into -- make sure that I -- yes, "sovereign and effective government," my apology, "and direct subordination to international law." Can you explain further or comment further to the Judges on that statement and the roles that those three considerations in particular play in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: I made this part of my report or analysis in the following way. I looked at the textbooks on the theory of state that were used by the law schools, in some law schools, particularly in Zagreb, Sarajevo, Ljubljana, all those textbooks are quoted, and I have to say that the professors who teach theory of the law of state, statehood, are in agreement as to the minimal elements that have to be in place for a new state to come into being. So this might be quite interesting. The only interesting point is the fourth element, so territory, population, and effective government are used by practically all the theorists but the fourth element was taken from a book entitled, "The State." It was published in 1927 in Ljubljana. The author is Professor Leonid Pitamic and as early as at that time, so it's really quite early, he noticed that states are increasingly dependent on international law and that their independence and sovereignty has indeed become relative, and it is his position that this does not pose a threat to the sovereignty and independence of the states if, under the international law, they are subjected directly -- if they are subjected to the international law directly and not through some other state. So I think that this is an element that is quite interesting in light of the analysis that I made concerning Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, in the analysis that you prepared, I seem to find something missing when you're talking about attributes of a state, the recognizance by other states. Why did you not mention that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mention this in other places. It is quite well known that there are states in existence, states that exist for quite some time before they achieve international recognition and before they join international organisations. In other words, before they are recognised by other states and international organisations. This is why I considered that this element, although it is indeed significant, is not at the same level of significance as the minimal elements that have to be there if we are to talk about the creation of a new state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand. But in the current world, a state that is comprised of a population, that population has a certain culture, if that state is not recognised by other states, should we not think that there is a problem there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. There is a problem. So you're absolutely right that if we look at things in long term -- on a long-term basis, it is hard to imagine that there could be a state in existence for a long time without being recognised internationally, but if we look at the situation in which new states are emerging, especially if you have an imminent threat of war, a military threat, then, in many cases, the analysis shows that the state came into being long before it was actually internationally recognised. And if we were to look at the emergence of the new states in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we can see that from the time when these minimum elements were in place, and to the time when they were recognised by other states and international organisations, it took some time. So quite sometime elapsed between the two points. In some cases longer, in some cases shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add a question: Professor, it would seem to me that being directly a subject of international law, because that is your fourth point, I think, being immediately bound by international law, is that not rather a consequence of the prerequisites for statehood being given than a condition, in the sense that first you have to find out if an entity can qualify as a state? If it can qualify as a state, then, as a consequence, it is submitted to international law directly rather than vice versa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When new states emerge, they would have to be subject to international law as soon as they start to emerge. In the process of their emergence, they, the new states, should comply with the basic principles of basic tenets of international law. So from that point of view, I could hardly agree with the argument that the direct subjection to international law is something that follows, that comes later. So in the very process of the emergence of a new state, the new state has to take into account certain rules, tenets and legal instruments that it has to comply with, it has to apply in its territory to its population, and the government has to take that into account and has to subject itself to international law in the very process of its creation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, because of course the subject is very broad and we could spend hours on it. When the Republic of Herceg-Bosna declared its independence and when it was not recognised as an independent state, since you are an expert in constitutional matters, can we make a parallel here with Taiwan, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards Herceg-Bosna, once it became a republic of Herceg-Bosna, it defined itself as a state community, not a state. It was done at the time when it seemed realistically to expect that it would be a member state or constituent state of some kind of federal or confederal Bosnia-Herzegovina. As regards Taiwan, I am not all that familiar with its position but I think that there we are dealing with the situation where a state community meets the requirements for a state but there are certain restrictions there that there are some time limitations for that -- that will affect the actual status of that state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, please continue. I'm terribly sorry for interrupting with these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No problem, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could just ask you then to move on to page 7 in the English part of your report, at page 6 in the Croatian version, to the topic of territory and population, and if we look on that, the first paragraph under the heading 2.2, "Territory and Population of the HZ HB," you make reference to the decision on establishing the HZ HB adopted on 18 November 1991. Can you explain the significance of that document with respect to your consideration of the territorial claims, if you will, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. When Herceg-Bosna was established, in this decision, it defined its territory. It listed the 30 municipalities and the representatives from those municipalities, representatives who had been elected on the HDZ platform and in some cases there were also representatives of this party. They all got together, and they established the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So we are talking about the 30 municipalities that make part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the immediately following that paragraph -- the next paragraph, excuse me, and I don't know if it changes the page in the Croatian version or not but it's the immediately following paragraph, still on page 7 of the English version, you state in your report: "The text of the decision does not explicitly indicate the criteria for determining the HZ HB territory." And then you go on from there. Can you comment further to the Chamber about what you found then in the course of preparing your report about what appeared to you to be the various considerations at work in the selection of those particular municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I immediately asked myself that question: Why the 30 municipalities? If the criteria were the Croatian majority in those municipalities, in other words, that Croats were in the majority in the population in those 30 municipalities then there would be no further questions but it is quite clear if we look at the data that are at our disposal that in some of those municipalities, quite a few of them, Croats were in the majority but there were also municipalities in which Croats were in the relative majority but they also included municipalities where ethnic Croats were in the minority. Other sources, particularly the transcripts of the meetings of the Herceg-Bosna leaders, the meeting that was held in Zagreb on the 27th of December 1991, indicate that when Herceg-Bosna was established, a major role was -- a major factor was the -- whether territory was part of the Banovina territory in 1939; Banovina was a creation that was established two years before the Second World War. Banovina Hvratska as it was styled, covered the very same territory of the 30 municipalities that were included in Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that respect, if then we could go on to the immediately next paragraph of your report, we are now on page 8, the paragraph beginning on page 8 of the English report, again on -- in this instance I'm not sure about the Croatian page but it's the following paragraph, you make this statement: "The selection of these 30 municipalities was obviously governed by certain historical and programmatic considerations." Could you comment to the Chamber or explain to the Chamber please what you mean by when you use the terminology "programmatic considerations"?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Well, what was obviously at play here was that the founders of Herceg-Bosna considered this to be the territory that belonged to the Croatian people historically speaking, and that for this reason, those parts of the territory should become part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I explain here in some footnotes that this was the territory that was part of Banovina Hvratska and I quote the view or the belief that this was territory that was lost in an unjust development after the Second World War. This is quite important, I posit, because we can see that Banovina Hvratska is mentioned in the preamble to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in particular, looking at page 8 in the English version we can see that at footnote 25; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: And 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could I then next ask you to look at, in your binders, what will be in your tab as 109?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Professor, I just noticed something, something that was already heard by other witnesses. You said in the preamble to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia there is a mention, and they refer to the Banovina Hvratska. On page 22 of line 35, this is what you say. So if I understand correctly, the constitution of the Republic of Croatia mentions this in its preamble and they refer very clearly to the Banovina Hvratska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now when Croatia became a recognised state, recognised by the international community, the international community knew very well the constitution of Croatia, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Banovina of Croatia was established in 1939. The reason was the attempt to prevent anything that might have led to conflicts among the nations as a result of the justified dissatisfaction of the Croats with their position in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In 1939, Banovina of Croatia was established and obviously this included the present state of Croatia as well as the territory that would subsequently become the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The preamble of the constitution mentions Banovina of Croatia in the place where the constitution speaks about its historical development, which is not unusual. I believe that the reference to the Independent State of Croatia, the so-called NDH, might be more in dispute than the reference being made to Banovina Croatia which is a fact, even from the legal and constitutional aspects, so the reference to the Banovina is nothing in dispute when it comes to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. It shouldn't be challenged from any aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talk of the constitution, a preamble has the same value as the article of the constitution or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I happened to write an article about the function of a preamble which was published not only in Slovenia but also in Sarajevo, in Bosniak language, and there I have analysed the different practices in the world with regard to the function of a preamble. By and large, it is believed that a preamble may be used as the foundation for the interpretation of the contents of constitutional provisions but there are also theoreticians who believe that a preamble may also have a binding effect. From that point of view, I would like to refer you to a constitution -- a decision of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina which, pursuant to the preamble of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina made null and void some provisions of the constitution of Republika Srpska, which referred to the position of the constituent peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But we also have other examples in the world. The decisions of the highest judicial bodies which evoked the constitutional preambles, especially in the cases when the preamble contained something that is very important for a state, which is not mentioned in any of the provisions of the constitution. This was, for example, the case in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A similar thing happened in France because the constitution there failed to mention the rights and freedoms, whereas the preamble referred to the declaration of human rights, and so on and so forth. In other words, the significance of a preamble may be great. In this particular case, in the case of -- in the case of Croatia, the preamble was similar to what Macedonia had at the time. Bosnia does not have such provisions and I'm talking about the provisions which speak about the historical development of significance for the particular state. In other words, the meaning of what is written cannot be used as the grounds for some territorial pretensions of one state towards another. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hopefully we can maybe finish on one or two questions further on this particular topic before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the background in mind of what you've told us, Professor, in the last few minutes, can I ask you, please, to look at 109 in your binder? For the record, Exhibit P 00109. And while you're doing that, finding that, I'll just simply state for the record this is Opinion number 3 of the Arbitration Commission of the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia, more commonly known perhaps as the Badinter Commission. An opinion that was issued on the 1st of November 1992. If you have that, sir, can I ask to you look to -- on the second page I'll refer again to the English document, on the second page, there are a number of numbered paragraphs, paragraph first, paragraph second, paragraph third. If I can ask to you look at paragraph second, it says: "The boundaries between Croatia and Serbia, between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia and possibly between other adjacent independent states may not be altered except by agreement freely arrived at." Can you comment on that opinion and that language in relation to your consideration of Herceg-Bosna's territorial claims?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: This position of the international community, namely that boundaries may be changed only pursuant to agreements freely arrived at and not in any other way, against the will of a party, is very significant, a very significant opinion, which has a bearing on the different situations that took place and that are still taking place when new states are being established. The arbitrary -- arbitration commission made a big difference between the declaration of independence on the part of certain republics and the right of the peoples to self-decision to secession, and a different opinion when it came to the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the peoples that existed within one of the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Their right to self-determination was considered differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understand correctly, Mr. Badinter that everybody knows, who presented this opinion, said the following: Is it to understand that when two states are in agreement, they can change boundaries? Is that what he wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was said was clearly said by the Badinter Commission, i.e., the commission headed by Badinter, and not only of his personal opinion. And I believe that it would be fair to conclude that boundaries could not be changed in any other way but by agreements reached through negotiations. There is no precise reference as to who the parties to the agreement are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But let's imagine, for a few seconds, that the Republic of Croatia and that the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed on certain changes between Tudjman and Izetbegovic to change the border or the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina by removing Herzegovina and by moving it on to the territory of the Republic of Croatia. According to the public international law should we think that this would be a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Badinter Commission, I agree with you, discussed only the issue that I'm not an expert in, i.e., the issue of boundaries and the issue of international law that involve states. If an agreement were to be reached, obviously some internal issues are being raised such as the issue of constitution. According to the constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in effect at the time, it was stipulated that the boundaries could only be changed only if that was so decided by the parliament pursuant to a referendum during which two-thirds of all the electorate body would be in changing the boundaries. I am not sure what was the constitutional order of Croatia at the time but I'm sure that Croatia made it sure that there were guarantees that its boundaries could not be changed so easily. For example, this could not have been done only by the presidents of the republics alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, as far as you know, since you are the specialist here, since the Yalta agreements, do you know whether some states have agreed to change their boundaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we are talking at cross-purposes. I have just said that I'm not an expert in international law; I am an expert only in constitutional law. When it comes to negotiations and agreements during the Second World War, it would be very hard for me to talk about the way boundaries were changed at the time. I'm familiar with the case that came to the European Court of Human Rights, when the boundary was changed between the Soviet Union and Poland, and at the same time, Poland received part of the German territory. How this was done during the Second World War, and after, that is not something that I would gladly talk about, but I believe that when it comes to the dealing with the problems in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, it is of some significance that this arbitration commission, as an independent body, composed of the best experts who also held the highest judicial positions within their respective states, determined certain principles that arise from international laws and lay down some principles as regards to boundaries that all those involved in dealing with the boundary issues had to comply with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time has come for a break. You know they stop selling coffee at 4.00. So we are going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Scott. Before you proceed, the court deputy has to give us an IC number belatedly. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. One of the parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness BB: The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 744. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just correct before we move off Exhibit P 00109, just so the record is clear, I think I -- before the break I reverted to the American conventions for dates, and I misstated the date. The date of the document although it says so right under the title was not November 1st, 1992, but the 11th of January 1992. Just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Professor, if I can next direct your attention, please, to page 13 of your report, and I believe it's on page 11 of the Croatian version, and in this respect, we are assisted because in your report you've actually underlined the particular language. It says, "The HZ HB proceeds from the premise of a mono-national Croatian state which does not guarantee non-Croats any special individual or collective minority rights." And I also would ask to you look at page 18 of your report, page 14 of the Croatian version. And on that page, you also state that non-Croats were treated as or viewed as second-class citizens under the HZ HB. You say it was because the HZ HB was not their state. Can you comment further on the basis for making those statements in your report?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this is connected with the question that we already discussed, i.e., the question of the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the reference made to the historical Croatian territories that we have already discussed when the Banovina of Croatia was mentioned. In other words, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established as a community that should have protected the rights of the Croatian people within Bosnia and Herzegovina. In some documents, it is stated that it would also protect the rights of those Croats who did not have residence in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. The way it was established was that at the meeting at which this community was established, representatives were present who had been elected from the list of the Croatian Democratic Union which means that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established as a mono-national community and that its bodies were also the same. Some even say that this was a mono-party formation given the role of the Croatian Democratic Union during its establishment. Based on the elements of the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, I am very critical to this state because such a community, which puts the interests of one people in the foreground, according to some democratic standards which prevail in the modern world, should give a special place to the protection of the rights of those people and groups of people who are not of Croatian ethnic origin. I must admit that when I was reading the documents issued by the Croatian Community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna I did not find any provisions that would be directly discriminating against those who were not of Croatian origin, but very late and very few and far between were those provisions that positively spoke about the obligation of that community to protect the rights of those people who did not belong to the body of the Croatian people in that community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you say is important. However, it raises a legal issue. Normally speaking, a constitution has effects on all the citizens of a given country, each and every citizen being equal to their fellow citizens, they must enjoy in the same way as other citizens what is agreed in the constitution. I'm not aware of your country's constitution but I suppose that you too have minority groups. I'm not at all aware of your constitution. Normally, though, in a constitution that does not mention any minorities explicitly, in law, the inhabitant, the resident, who is a citizen, a national, of that country, does he not have the same rights no matter what his ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we are talking about a community for which it may be said that to a certain extent it might have been an attempt to create a new state or a state community. However, its development did not go that far so as to formalise the issue of the statehood of those who lived in Herceg-Bosna. However, it was believed that all the inhabitants of that area of Herceg-Bosna had and enjoyed the same position and rights. What I'm talking about is the fact that when Herceg-Bosna was being established, and when its bodies were being established, the protection of the historical rights of the Croatian people came into the foreground as a priority and that's why the bodies of that community were mono-national in their composition. In other words, the foundations were democratic elections. However, when it came to the establishing the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, only those representatives that were elected from the list of the Croatian Democratic Union made it to the Presidency, which means that the basis for the establishment of that supreme organ in that community was mono-national. This gives a more acute perspective to the issue of equality of other inhabitants of that community. In order for them not to feel as citizens of the second rank in that community, they should have given -- been given even more rights. In Slovenia, members of national minorities, particularly the Italian and Hungarian minorities as well as the Roma population, enjoyed -- enjoy special rights which means that citizens that belong to those minorities enjoy the rights that are enjoyed by other citizens but they also have additional, individual and collective rights, which amongst other things implies that the representatives of Italian and Hungarian communities are represented by the state parliament. What I'm saying is that under such conditions, a state in the making, which is trying to become an independent state, such a state should provide in its most important documents provisions on the special rights and position of members of other peoples and national minorities. The then-prevailing constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a broad range of provisions that provided for the rights of the three constituent peoples and members of other peoples and national minorities that resided in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. So this should not have been a novelty or a particular exception to the rule that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... discover that there are ethnic minorities in your country, for instance, Italians and Hungarians who enjoy specific or special rights, but did you not tend to apply the Slovenian mode of operation to the analysis you made of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did draw a comparison, and in my analysis I pointed to the differences. One of the major differences, very important ones, is relative to this particular issue. When the Republic of Slovenia became independent, all the inhabitants of Slovenia, i.e., all those who had permanent residence in Slovenia at the moment, even if they originated from other republics and they were not Slovenians by origin had the right to vote in the plebiscite for the independence of Slovenia. In addition to that, Slovenia guaranteed to them that they would be entitled to Slovenian citizenship without any other basis for that but the basis that they had permanent residence in Slovenia at the time. The results of the plebiscite showed that many of them voted in favour of the independence of Slovenia although they were not nationals of Slovenia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We understood perfectly. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you actually addressed a number of other questions that I would put to you. You mentioned for example the role of the HDZ political party. So I'll move on from that. But let me go to page 16 of your report, page 13 in the Croatian version. On the bottom of page 16 of the English version, you make reference to something called "SAO-isation". Can you explain to the Judges what you mean and perhaps put that further in context and what you meant by reference to "SAO-isation"?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. This term, "SAO-isation" referred to the establishment of Serb autonomous regions. This is something that happened both in the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was a process whereby the Serb people organised themselves in special territorial units. Croatia, unlike Slovenia, for instance, had a substantial part of territory that was inhabited by ethnic Serbs, and Croatia deemed that the establishment of Serb autonomous regions in its territory is, in fact, a basis for the secession of these parts of its territory from Croatia and their annexation to Serbia or rather that this was a basis for the establishment of the so-called Greater Serbia. I would like to stress here something that I've put in my report, too, and that is that the constitutional court of the Republic of Croatia, in 1990, annulled the decision on the establishment of such communities, the community of municipalities of Northern Dalmacija and Lika, ruling that the decisions to establish those communities were unconstitutional and illegal or rather that they were not based on the constitution and the law, and furthermore, they were not published, and that was also one of the prerequisites for a legal decision to be valid. As regards the organisation of those territorial units on the part of Serbs, Croatia saw that as an attempt to have those territories secede from the Republic of Croatia. The representatives of Croats and Bosniaks held the same view regarding the establishment of the Serb autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is something that is surprising in this light, because something that is branded as unacceptable on the one hand is being pursued and the same methods are being used to ensure special status for a certain part of the territory. And that is why I think that we can say that the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is something that came about as a consequence of the SAO-isation, something that followed on it, and something that can have the same negative consequences as the establishment of the Serb autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can now move on to another one of the principal factors that you listed in your report and that we briefly discussed at the beginning of your testimony, and that is government, on page 18 of your report, in the English version, and on page 15 of the Croatian report, in the first paragraph under 2.3, you talk about there being two phases in reference to the bodies of the HZ HB and you say: "The first phase began with the establishment of the HZ HB (18th November 1991) and lasted until the establishment on 8 April 1992 of the Croatian Defence Council and its constitution at the municipal and HZ HB levels. The second phase lasted until the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna (28 August 1993)." Now in talking about the structures of the government in that context and focusing for a moment on what you've called the first phase, can you tell the Judges what was the principal governmental body in reference to the entity Herceg-Bosna in the first phase, as you've described it?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the first phase, Herceg-Bosna had a rather simple organisation. There was the concentration of power in the hands of a single body, and its officials. The body was called the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and the Presidency, and in particular four of its officials, held in their hands all the power in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So no other bodies of executive and administrative government were established, because all those elements that would be in the hands of the parliament, the government, the head of state in a normal state, that was all concentrated in the hands of the Presidency, the president, the two vice-presidents and the secretary of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna so that was what the situation was like until the HVO was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to be very, very clear in telling us or describing which Presidency you're talking about? Because the Judges in this case, in fact all of us, have heard the term Presidency used in a number of different contexts. You just identified four positions, the president, two vice-presidents and secretary of the Presidency. If I can put names to those and then can you confirm to me is that the Presidency you're talking about? Mr. Boban being the president, Bozo Rajic being one of the vice-presidents at that time, Dario Kordic being another vice-president at that time, and Ignac Kostroman being the secretary of the Presidency; are those the four individuals you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the top officials in the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. These are the people that are referred to when you talk about the leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So these are the leaders. And the members are representatives of the 30 municipalities that comprised the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. But one has to add that very early on, the function of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna became independent from the Presidency. So Mr. Boban was not only the president of the Presidency but very early on in this first stage he became the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but in this first phase those functions were not clearly delineated yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. But, again, just to be very clear, when you talk about this first phase, and that is for approximately November 1991 until April 1992, when you refer in your report to the Presidency being the dominant governmental body, you're talking about this Presidency made up of Boban, Rajic, Kordic and Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me move forward then to what you described as the second phase, from the creation of the HVO on or about the 8th of April 1992 to the establishment of the republic at the end of August 1993. Can you tell the Judges how the governing structures of Herceg-Bosna changed, if they did, during the second phase and how that evolution took place?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Well, we could say that once the HVO was established, the executive and administrative functions became separate from the functions of the Presidency. The HVO was set up as some kind of a government, an emerging government, and we could say that this is a natural second phase. So operational responsibilities for the implementation of the decisions was now in the hands of the HVO, which was organised in the following manner. Or it was organised in such a manner that we can really say that it resembled a normal government. It had bodies, departments, some members are responsible for certain areas, which are parallel to ministers in normal governments, but we have to say here that the HVO remained subordinate to the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and that the Presidency had substantial powers over the HVO, both in terms of issuing guidelines for its work and also in terms of the power of veto over any decisions reached by the HVO. So I think that there was a shift in the relationship there, and that the position of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and its presidents -- president, actually weakened but it has to be stressed at the same time that the Presidency retained quite a lot of its original powers, and the Presidency also retained the control over the operation of the HVO. At a later stage, the HVO, in addition to what is considered normal for an executive body to do, on some occasions took decisions that are normally taken by a House of Representatives, a parliament in a normal state but I don't think that it is such an oddity in fact because these were exceptional circumstances, after all. We are talking about a war or threat of war. And even in established democracies some powers are conferred on the executive in such circumstances too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me come back to a couple of things you've just said in a few moments but before we move forward in time, because we were talking about the second phase beginning in approximately April of 1992, can I ask you, please, to turn to what you will find at tab 297, which is Exhibit P 00297. You have that, sir. Can I ask to you look at that and this appears to be the appointment of Bruno Stojic as head of the Defence Department of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna dated the 3rd of July 1992 over the name of Mate Boban. And I note in this particular decision Mr. Boban apparently is described as the president at this time of the HVO and the HZ HB. Can you comment on that and how long that continued to be the case?

utterances.speaker: CIRIL RIBICIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the first phase, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was at the same time the president of the HVO. This situation lasted a couple of months, until August, in fact, which was when another man was appointed the president of the HVO so it was no longer the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna by virtue of his office.
